sections.title: 0. The big picture
sections.html:
• module = one .py file with definitions (functions, variables, classes) you can import.
  • package = a folder of modules (+ an __init__.py). Module : package = file : folder.
  • standard library = all modules shipped with Python (math, random, platform, sys, os…) = a library where modules are the books.
  • PyPI = the online repo of free packages ("The Cheese Shop"); pip = the tool that installs them.
  • Exam questions here are mostly "what is printed?" and "which import is valid?".

sections.title: 1. The 4 ways to import
sections.html:
formwhat enters YOUR namespacehow you call pi
import mathonly the name mathmath.pi
from math import pi, sinonly pi and sinpi
import math as monly m (math is NOT defined!)m.pi
from math import *every public name of mathpi
  • namespace = the space where names live; inside one namespace each name is unique.
  • import math → math's names do not enter your namespace → your own pi is safe. You must qualify: math.pi.
  • from math import pi → pi enters your namespace and can overwrite (or be overwritten by) your own pi.
  • Several modules: import math, sys or one per line (preferred).
  • Many aliases at once: from module import n as a, m as b.
♥ Learn by heart
  • After import math as m the name math is inaccessible → math.pi = NameError.
  • as is a keyword. The alias replaces the name, it does not add a second one.
  • Last assignment wins: a later from … import pi overwrites your pi, and your later pi = … overwrites the imported one.
⚠ Trap
from math import * imports every name except the ones starting with _. It is risky: it can silently overwrite your names. Don't use it in real code, but know it for the exam.

asks.code:
import math as m
print(m.floor(2.7))
print(math.floor(2.7))
asks.why: after aliasing, only m exists.

asks.code:
from math import pi
pi = 3
print(pi)
asks.why: your assignment comes after the import, so it wins.

asks.code:
pi = 3
from math import pi
print(pi)
asks.why: the import comes last, so it overwrites your pi.

asks.code:
def sin(x):
    return "mine"
import math
print(sin(0), math.sin(0))
asks.why: import math doesn't touch your namespace; math.sin(0) returns a float.

asks.code:
from m import *
print(a)
print(_b)
asks.why: * skips names beginning with an underscore.

sections.title: 2. dir() – what's inside a module
sections.html:
• dir(module) returns an alphabetically sorted list of all names in the module.
  • Module must be imported first with import math (not from math import …), otherwise dir(math) → NameError.
  • Works in the console too: import math then dir(math).

asks.q: What is the type of the result?
asks.code:
import math
print(type(dir(math)).__name__)

from math import pi
print(dir(math))
asks.why: only pi was imported, the name math does not exist.

sections.title: 6. Writing your own module
sections.html:
• Put module.py and main.py in the same folder; main.py does import module.
  • First import → Python creates __pycache__/module.cpython-3x.pyc: semi-compiled code (not machine code), so later imports are faster. Rebuilt automatically if the source changes.
  • When imported, the module's code is executed (initialization) — only once, at the first import. Later imports are silently skipped.
  • Every file has its own variable __name__.
♥ Learn by heart
  • Run the file directly → __name__ == "__main__"
  • Imported as a module → __name__ == "module" (file name without .py)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("run directly: do some tests")
else:
    print("I was imported")
  • Private variables? Python can't hide module variables. Convention only: start the name with _ or __ = "please don't touch". Users can still read/modify it.
  • To change a module-level variable inside a function you need global __counter.
  • #!/usr/bin/env python3 = shebang: a comment for Python, but tells Unix/macOS which program runs the file.
  • A string at the top of the module = doc-string: explains the module.

sections.title: 7. Where does Python look? sys.path
sections.html:
• sys.path is a list of folders searched in order during an import.
  • First element = the folder of the script you started.
  • First folder that contains the module wins; the others are ignored. Not found anywhere → ModuleNotFoundError (an ImportError).
  • It can contain a .zip file: Python treats zips like folders.
  • Add a folder: sys.path.append('..\\modules') (goes last) or sys.path.insert(0, path) (goes first).
⚠ Trap
Windows paths in strings need double backslashes: "C:\\Users\\user\\py\\modules" (or use /). A relative path like '..\\modules' only works if you start from the right folder.

asks.q: Course exercise 2: modules are in D:\Python\Project\Modules. Make Python search there.

asks.code:
import sys
print(type(sys.path).__name__)
import modul_that_does_not_exist
asks.why: it is a subclass of ImportError, so except ImportError catches it.

sections.title: 8. Packages
sections.html:
• A package is a folder of modules (and sub-packages). Names use dots like folders: extra.good.best.tau.funT().
  • __init__.py makes the folder a package. It is executed when any module of the package is imported (package initialization). It can be empty, but must not be omitted (course rule).
  • Sub-folders can have their own __init__.py too.
  • The package's parent folder must be on sys.path.
extra/                    # package
  __init__.py
  iota.py                 # funI()
  good/                   # sub-package
    __init__.py
    alpha.py   beta.py
    best/  __init__.py  sigma.py  tau.py   # funT()
  ugly/  __init__.py  psi.py  omega.py
♥ Learn by heart
Three valid ways to call funT():
import extra.good.best.tau
extra.good.best.tau.funT()

from extra.good.best.tau import funT
funT()

import extra.good.best.tau as t
t.funT()
Wrong: import tau (no full path) → ModuleNotFoundError.

asks.q: extra/__init__.py prints 'extra init', extra/iota.py defines funI() returning 'Iota'. What is printed?
asks.code:
import extra.iota
print(extra.iota.funI())

import extra.iota
print(iota.funI())
asks.why: import extra.iota only defines the name extra; you must write the full path.

asks.ans: import abc.def.mymodule (then abc.def.mymodule.something; in real Python def is a keyword, but this is the course's answer).

sections.title: 1. Characters are numbers
sections.html:
• A computer stores every character as a number. Some are whitespaces, some are control characters (invisible, control devices).
  • code point = the number that makes a character. Ex: 32 = space, 65 = 'A', 97 = 'a'.
  • ASCII = most used code. Room for 256 chars, but the standard part is the first 128 (Latin letters, digits, signs).
  • I18N (internationalization: I + 18 letters + N) = software usable in every language/alphabet.
  • code page = a standard that uses the upper 128 code points (128–255) for national characters → the same code point can mean different characters in different code pages.
  • Unicode = the long-term solution: unique characters for more than a million code points. First 128 = ASCII; first 256 = ISO/IEC 8859-1 (Western Europe).
  • Unicode only names characters; storing them is done by an encoding:
encodinghow it storesremember
UCS-432 bits (4 bytes) for every charUniversal Character Set; simple, wastes space; may start with a BOM
UTF-8as many bits as needed (1 to 4 bytes)Unicode Transformation Format; most used; ASCII chars take 8 bits
♥ Learn by heart
  • BOM (Byte Order Mark) = invisible bits at the start of a file announcing its encoding (UCS-4, UTF-8…).
  • Python 3 is fully I18Ned: Unicode/UTF-8 in variable names and in all input/output.
  • ord('a') = 97 · chr(97) = 'a' · ord('A') = 65 · ord(' ') = 32 · ord('0') = 48.
  • Uppercase letters have smaller codes than lowercase: 'Z' (90) < 'a' (97).

asks.why: ord() needs a one-character string.

sections.title: 2. Strings are immutable sequences
sections.html:
• Multiline strings use triple quotes; the line break inside counts as one character \n.
  • Indexing s[0], negative s[-1], slices s[1:4], s[::-1], for ch in s: all work like lists.
  • + concatenates (order matters, not commutative); * repeats ('ab'*3 = 3*'ab').
  • in / not in look for a substring anywhere: 'f' in 'abcdef'.
♥ Learn by heart
Immutable = you can never change a string in place:
  • s[0] = 'X' → TypeError
  • del s[0] → TypeError (but del s deletes the whole variable: OK)
  • s.append('x'), s.insert(…) → AttributeError (strings have no such methods)
  • Every method (upper, replace…) returns a new string; the original stays the same.
⚠ Trap
len('\n') = 1 (one escape char) but len('\\n') = 2 (backslash + n). A backslash at the very end of a string 'abc\' → SyntaxError.

sections.title: 5. Comparing strings
sections.html:
• Compared character by character using code points; the first difference decides.
  • If one string is the start of the other, the shorter is smaller: 'alpha' < 'alphabet'.
  • Uppercase < lowercase: 'beta' > 'Beta'. Digits < uppercase < lowercase.
  • Digits in strings are compared as text, not as numbers: '10' < '8' is True ('1' < '8').
♥ Learn by heart
  • string == number → always False; != → always True (no error).
  • string < > <= >= number → TypeError.

sections.title: 1. What is an exception?
sections.html:
• When Python doesn't know what to do with your code it: (1) stops the program and (2) creates a special object called an exception. Both together = raising an exception.
  • If nobody handles it → the program ends with a traceback, e.g. ValueError: math domain error.
  • 1/0 → ZeroDivisionError · [][0] → IndexError · {}['k'] → KeyError · int('x') → ValueError · 'a'+1 → TypeError · undefined_name → NameError · obj.nothing → AttributeError.

sections.title: 2. try / except
sections.html:
try:
    risky code            # stops at the FIRST error
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("can't divide by 0")
except ValueError:
    print("not an integer")
except:                   # anything else (must be LAST)
    print("something went wrong")
print("THE END.")
♥ Learn by heart
  • Python checks the except branches top to bottom and runs only the first one that matches. The others are skipped.
  • A branch matches if the exception is that class or a subclass of it.
  • The bare except: must be the last branch (otherwise SyntaxError). It equals except BaseException:.
  • Several exceptions in one branch: except (ValueError, TypeError): — parentheses required.
  • If no branch matches, the exception continues upward (and may stop the program).
⚠ Trap
except: placed before another except is a SyntaxError (the program doesn't even start). try needs at least one except or a finally.

asks.code:
try:
    print('1')
    x = 1 / 0
    print('2')
except:
    print('Oh dear, something went wrong...')
print('3')
asks.why: '2' is never printed: the try block stops at the error.
ArithmeticError is the parent of ZeroDivisionError, it matches first; the 'zero' branch is dead code.
no branch matches → unhandled → 'end' is never printed.

asks.ans: SyntaxError: default 'except:' must be last. Nothing runs at all.

sections.html: • An exception raised in a function can be handled inside it, or it travels up to the caller (and the caller's caller…) until a matching except is found.

sections.title: 5. raise, bare raise, assert
sections.html:
• raise ZeroDivisionError or raise ValueError('message'): raise an exception yourself (to test your handlers, or to pass part of the handling to someone else).
  • Bare raise (no name) — only inside an except branch: re-raises the same exception.
  • Bare raise outside any except → RuntimeError.
  • assert expression: does nothing if the expression is true (non-zero, non-empty, not None); otherwise raises AssertionError. Think of it as an airbag.

sections.title: 6. else and finally
sections.html:
try:      ...   # risky
except:   ...   # only if an exception happened
else:     ...   # only if NO exception happened
finally:  ...   # ALWAYS, no matter what
♥ Learn by heart
  • Order is fixed: try → except(s) → else → finally. else must come after the last except.
  • finally runs even if the exception was not handled, and even if the try/except did return.
  • If finally has its own return, it overrides the other return.

sections.title: 7. Exceptions are objects (classes)
sections.html:
• Raising an exception = creating an object of an exception class. Catch it with except ValueError as e:.
  • print(e) = print(e.__str__()) = the message.
  • e.args = tuple of the arguments given to the constructor: raise Exception('a', 'b') → ('a', 'b').
  • No argument → args == () and str(e) == ''. One argument → str(e) is that argument. Several → str(e) looks like the tuple.
⚠ Trap
e.args is filled with what you passed to the constructor even if your own __init__ doesn't call the parent's.
  • Exception classes know their tree: ZeroDivisionError.__bases__ → (ArithmeticError,); BaseException.__subclasses__() lists the children (course's print_exception_tree walks the tree recursively).

sections.html:
• Create one by inheriting from an existing exception (usually Exception): class MyError(Exception): pass.
  • It fits in the tree: except ParentError also catches your subclass.
  • Add data by overriding __init__ and calling the parent: Exception.__init__(self, message) or super().__init__(message).
  • Put the more specific class first in the except list.

  • Each object has: a name (identifies it), a set of properties (can be empty), a set of methods (can be empty).
  • Inheritance diagram: superclasses above, arrows go from subclass to superclass.
  • Procedural approach: data and functions separate (e.g. a global list + push/pop functions). Object approach: data + methods packed together in a class → several independent stacks, hidden data, reuse by inheritance.

sections.title: 2. The Stack: constructor, self, private
sections.html:
class Stack:
    def __init__(self):                # constructor
        self.__stack_list = []         # private property
    def push(self, val):
        self.__stack_list.append(val)
    def pop(self):
        val = self.__stack_list[-1]
        del self.__stack_list[-1]
        return val

stack_object = Stack()                 # create an object
stack_object.push(3)                   # Python sends stack_object as self
♥ Learn by heart
  • The constructor is always named __init__; it runs automatically when you create the object; it builds the object's properties.
  • Every method needs at least one parameter, conventionally self = the object it is called on. You never pass self yourself when calling obj.method().
  • A property is created the first time you assign it: self.x = ….
  • Name starting with __ (and not ending with __) = private: obj.__stack_list from outside → AttributeError.
  • Public name: no leading __, at most one trailing _.

asks.code:

    def pop(self):

        return val

little_stack = Stack()
another_stack = Stack()
funny_stack = Stack()
little_stack.push(1)
another_stack.push(little_stack.pop() + 1)
funny_stack.push(another_stack.pop() - 2)
print(funny_stack.pop())
asks.why: 1 → 1+1 = 2 → 2-2 = 0. Each object has its own list.
Python passes the object automatically, but show has no parameter to receive it.

sections.title: 3. Subclass: AddingStack
sections.html:
class AddingStack(Stack):              # AddingStack inherits from Stack
    def __init__(self):
        Stack.__init__(self)           # MUST call the superclass constructor
        self.__sum = 0
    def get_sum(self):
        return self.__sum
    def push(self, val):               # overriding
        self.__sum += val
        Stack.push(self, val)          # call the superclass version
    def pop(self):
        val = Stack.pop(self)
        self.__sum -= val
        return val
♥ Learn by heart
  • Python does not call the superclass constructor for you: forget Stack.__init__(self) and the object has no __stack_list.
  • Calling through the class name Stack.push(self, val) → you must pass self explicitly. With super(): super().push(val) → no self.
  • Interface (method names) stays the same, implementation changes = overriding.

asks.why: Child's constructor never called Base's, so items was never created.

sections.title: 4. Instance variables & __dict__
sections.html:
• Instance variables belong to one object; different objects of the same class can have different sets of variables.
  • You can add one anytime, even from outside: obj.third = 5.
  • obj.__dict__ = a dictionary of the object's instance variables (name → value).

    def __init__(self, val = 1):
        self.first = val
    def set_second(self, val):

example_object_2.set_second(3)
example_object_3 = ExampleClass(4)
example_object_3.third = 5
print(example_object_1.__dict__)
print(example_object_2.__dict__)
print(example_object_3.__dict__)

sections.title: 5. Name mangling ("private" is not really private)
sections.html:
♥ Learn by heart
Inside a class, __name becomes _ClassName__name. So obj._ExampleClass__first works from outside. But a __name created outside the class (obj.__third = 5) is not mangled. Methods __m() are mangled the same way.

sections.title: 6. Class variables
sections.html:
• Defined in the class body (outside methods): one single copy shared by all objects; exists even before any object is created.
  • Not shown in obj.__dict__, but shown in ClassName.__dict__.
  • Read it through the class or through any object: ExampleClass.counter or obj.counter.
⚠ Trap
Writing through an object obj.counter = 9 does NOT change the class variable: it creates an instance variable with the same name that hides the class one (for that object only). To change the shared value write ClassName.counter = …. But a mutable class variable (list) changed with .append() is shared by everyone.

example_object_3 = ExampleClass(4)

sections.title: 7. Does it exist? hasattr()
sections.html:
• Reading an attribute that doesn't exist → AttributeError.
  • hasattr(obj_or_class, 'name') → True/False. The name is a string.
  • A class var is visible from the object (hasattr(obj, 'a') True), but an instance var is not visible from the class.

sections.title: 8. Methods in detail
sections.html:
• A method may be called without arguments, but never declared without a parameter (self).
  • Extra parameters go after self: def method(self, par) → call obj.method(1).
  • Through self a method reads instance and class variables (self.varia) and calls other methods (self.other()).
  • Constructors are functions: they can have default values: def __init__(self, value=None).

    def method(self):

sections.title: 12. super() and inherited properties
sections.html:
• super() reaches the superclass without naming it: super().__init__(name) (no self!).
  • Old way: Super.__init__(self, name) (with self).
  • Subclass objects see the superclass's class variables automatically; superclass instance variables exist only if the superclass constructor was called.

asks.why: Sub has no __str__, so Super's is used (inherited).

sections.title: 13. Multiple inheritance & the MRO
sections.html:
♥ Learn by heart
  • Python searches an attribute bottom → top (the object, its class, then superclasses) and stops at the first one found.
  • With several superclasses, it searches left → right in the order written: class Sub(Left, Right) → Left first.
  • This order = MRO (Method Resolution Order). See it with Sub.__mro__ or Sub.mro().
  • Diamond: D(B, C), B and C both from A → MRO D, B, C, A, object (A only after both B and C).
  • Impossible order → TypeError: Cannot create a consistent MRO.

asks.why: Top is listed before its own subclass Middle → no consistent MRO.

sections.title: 1. Iterators: the iterator protocol
sections.html:
• An object works in for x in obj if it follows the iterator protocol:
  • __iter__() → returns the iterator (usually self); called once at the start.
  • __next__() → returns the next value; when there is nothing left it must raise StopIteration (that ends the loop quietly).

asks.why: __next__ is called 7 times: 6 values + 1 StopIteration.

sections.title: 2. Generators: yield
sections.html:
• A function with yield is a generator: calling it does not run the body, it returns a generator object.
  • Each next() (or each loop turn) runs until the next yield, gives the value, and pauses (keeps its local variables). return would end everything.
  • You can loop on it, use it in a list comprehension, or convert it: list(gen()).
♥ Learn by heart
  • A generator is used up after one full pass: a second loop gives nothing.
  • next() on an exhausted generator → StopIteration.
  • len(gen) → TypeError. (x for x in …) with parentheses = a generator, brackets = a list.

asks.code:
def powers_of_2(n):
    power = 1
    for i in range(n):
        yield power
        power *= 2

t = [x for x in powers_of_2(5)]
print(t)
print(list(powers_of_2(3)))

def gen():
    yield 1
    yield 2

g = gen()
print(list(g), list(g))
asks.why: the second list(g) finds it already exhausted.

    yield 'a'

g = gen()
print(next(g))
print(next(g))

    print('start')
    yield 1

• Closure = a technique that stores values even though the context that created them no longer exists.
  • An inner function uses a variable of the outer function; the outer function returns the inner one; the returned function still remembers the variable.
  • Great for function factories: make many specialised functions from one template.

• Unix/Linux file names are case-sensitive; Windows keeps the case but ignores it.
  • Separators: \ on Windows, / on Unix. In Python strings write 'C:\\dir\\file' or simply 'C:/dir/file' (Python converts).
  • A program talks to files through a stream (handle). Opening = binding the stream to a file (first operation); closing = unbinding (last operation).
  • stream = open(file, mode='r', encoding=None): the only way to get a stream object (never a constructor). Fails → exception, e.g. FileNotFoundError.

sections.title: 10. Binary files: bytearray
sections.html:
• bytearray(10) = a mutable array of 10 bytes, all zeros. Acts like a list: len, indexing, loops.
  • Each element must be an int (else TypeError) in 0–255 (else ValueError).
  • Write: open('f.bin', 'wb').write(data).
  • Read into an existing bytearray: bf.readinto(data) (fills it, returns the number of bytes read).
  • bf.read() → a bytes object (like bytearray but immutable); bf.read(5) → at most 5 bytes.

sections.title: 12. datetime & time course
sections.html:
• date(2019, 11, 4), date.today(), .year .month .day.

  • date.fromisoformat('2019-11-04') (YYYY-MM-DD) · d.replace(year=1992) returns a new date.
  • d.weekday(): Monday = 0 … Sunday = 6 (isoweekday(): Monday = 1).

  • datetime(2019, 11, 4, 14, 53) → .date(), .time(), .timestamp(); datetime.today(), now(), utcnow().
  • time module: time.time(), time.sleep(s), ctime(ts) → string, gmtime(ts)/localtime(ts) → struct_time, asctime(st) → string, mktime(tuple) → seconds.

sections.html:
• calendar.calendar(2020) → string of the year (print it) · prcal(2020) prints it directly.

sections.title: A1. Loops with else
sections.html:
• for … else / while … else: the else block runs when the loop ends normally (condition false / items exhausted).
  • It does NOT run if the loop was left with break. Use: "search, and do something if not found".
  • A loop that never runs at all still runs its else.

sections.title: A2. match – case (Python 3.10+)
sections.html:
match command:
    case "start" | "go":          # | = several alternatives
        ...
    case ("move", x):            # pattern with capture
        ...
    case _:                      # default: matches anything
        ...
  • Compares one value with patterns top to bottom; runs the first matching case only (no fall-through, no break needed).
  • case _: is the default. Without it and with no match, nothing happens (no error).
  • Difference from if-elif: matches on the shape of data (tuples, lists, captures), not only on boolean conditions.

def describe(p):

        case (0, 0):
            return "origin"
        case (0, y):
            return f"on y axis at {y}"
        case (x, y) if x == y:
            return "diagonal"
        case _:
            return "somewhere"

sections.title: A4. More OOP: getattr, super() in multiple inheritance, safe __init__
sections.html:
• getattr(obj, 'name') reads an attribute by its string name; getattr(obj, 'x', default) gives default instead of AttributeError.
  • Cooperative multiple inheritance: super() calls the next class in the MRO, not necessarily the parent you think.
  • Validate arguments inside __init__ and raise ValueError / TypeError; use keyword arguments and sensible defaults.
⚠ Trap
Mutable default argument: def __init__(self, items=[]) — the same list is created once and shared by every object. Use items=None then self.items = items if items is not None else [].

sections.title: A5. Exceptions: raise e vs raise
sections.html:
• Inside except … as e: bare raise re-raises the current exception unchanged; raise e raises the same object again (explicitly); raise OtherError(…) replaces it.
  • except (A, B) as e works; the exception object's args property holds the arguments.

sections.title: A7. pip & requirements.txt
sections.html:
• python -m pip install requests = same as pip, but uses the pip of that Python.
  • pip freeze > requirements.txt records exact versions (requests==2.31.0); pip install -r requirements.txt rebuilds the same environment → reproducible.
  • PyPI packages = external; standard library = shipped with Python; local modules = your files.

sections.title: A9. Working in a team (Git)
sections.html:
• Shared repository: everyone works on the same code history.
  • Branch: isolate your change so others can work in parallel. Commit: a saved, described step (clear message: what + why).
  • Pull / merge request: propose merging your branch; teammates review it (specific, constructive comments); you answer and revise.
  • Merge conflict: two people changed the same lines → a human decides the final version; prevent with small changes and communication.
  • CI (continuous integration): runs the automated tests on every change; merge when review + tests are green. Issues / task records document bugs, requirements, decisions.

sections.title: A10. AI-assisted coding
sections.html:
• Give the AI clear requirements, context, examples, constraints; refine the prompt if the output is wrong or incomplete.
  • Human-in-the-loop (HITL): you review, test and approve every AI output before using it; you stay responsible.
  • Check correctness, readability, security; run and test generated code; verify that the functions/modules/APIs it mentions really exist (AI can invent them).
  • Never paste passwords, keys, personal data or proprietary code into an AI tool.

asks.q: An AI suggests import string_utils and calls string_utils.smart_title(). What should you do first?
asks.ans: Verify the module/function really exist and behave as claimed (docs, run it, tests) before using it: never trust it blindly.
